title: North Macedonia remains stalled on its EU path after 21 years as a candidate
summary: EU enlargement has regained momentum, with Montenegro and Albania moving closer to membership. But North Macedonia, a candidate since 2005, remains stalled by a politically difficult dispute…

image.caption: North Macedonia has been an EU candidate country for 21 years. Pictured here: Prime Minister of North Macedonia Hristijan Mickoski (right) with EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos in 2025Image: Petr Stojanovski/DW

blocks.text: The European Union's enlargement drive has regained momentum: Montenegro could become the bloc's 28th member in 2028, while Albania is rapidly advancing through accession talks and could complete accession negotiations by the end of 2027 if it maintains its current pace of reforms.
But North Macedonia, an EU candidate since 2005, remains stalled on the road to accession.
That contrast will be particularly evident at Wednesday's EU-Western Balkans summit in Brussels.

"The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union. Their accession is our priority, our shared ambition and a crucial geopolitical investment in these turbulent times," European Council President Antonio Costa said ahead of the meeting.
Prepared, but the handbrake is still on

North Macedonia formally opened accession talks with the EU in July 2022 but has yet to open the first of the EU's six negotiating clusters, the groups of policy areas through which candidates align their laws and institutions with EU standards.
But the lack of movement does not mean the country is unprepared for membership.

blocks.caption: 'The Western Balkans' future is in the European Union,' European Council President Antonio Costa said recently. Pictured here: European leaders gathered for the EU-Western Balkans Summit in JuneImage: Kay Nietfeld/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: EU Enlargement Commissioner Marta Kos said in November that North Macedonia was "among the countries with the highest level of preparedness" in aligning with EU law and had recently accelerated reforms under the EU Growth Plan.
However, she added, "the handbrake on its accession negotiations is still on."
Kos said that to release this handbrake and open the first cluster, North Macedonia must adopt the constitutional amendment agreed with the EU in 2022.
What's blocking N. Macedonia's EU progress?
The stalemate has deep roots.
For years, a dispute with Greece over the country's name blocked North Macedonia's progress along the EU accession path.
Although the 2018 Prespa Agreement resolved the dispute, and the country changed its constitutional name, clearing the way for NATO membership, a breakthrough on EU accession did not follow.

Bulgaria later blocked the process amid disputes over history, language and identity. A compromise brokered during the French EU presidency in 2022 lifted the veto but made further progress conditional on North Macedonia amending its constitution to explicitly include Bulgarians among the country's recognized communities.

blocks.caption: Gert Jan Koopman of the European Commission has said that North Macedonia is not blocked by an EU member state but 'is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done'Image: Ognen Teofilovski/REUTERS

blocks.text: The amendment requires a two-thirds majority in parliament, which has so far proved unattainable.
'Not blocked by a member state'
From the EU's perspective, this is no longer a Bulgarian veto, but a condition North Macedonia accepted as part of its negotiating framework.

"It [North Macedonia] is not blocked by a member state. It is blocked because it doesn't want to date to do what it knows needs to be done," Gert Jan Koopman, the European Commission's director-general for Neighbourhood and Enlargement Negotiations, recently told an Atlantic Council podcast.
North Macedonia's government sees the problem differently.
EU membership remains its declared strategic goal, but Skopje wants guarantees that amending its constitution will not simply pave the way for further demands from Sofia.

Those concerns are rooted partly in long-running disputes over identity and history: Bulgarian governments have challenged North Macedonia's interpretation of a centuries-old distinct Macedonian identity, while some Bulgarian politicians have gone further, describing Macedonian as a regional variant of Bulgarian, and Macedonians and Bulgarians as one people.

President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says North Macedonia is ready for talks with Bulgaria and the EU but wants certainty that one constitutional change will not simply be followed by demands for another.
"We only want certainty. We only want this not to be yet another amendment for the sake of an amendment, followed by another one," she said.
Strong support for membership, little appetite for compromise
After more than two decades of waiting, the deadlock has also become a domestic political problem in North Macedonia.

blocks.caption: North Macedonia's President Gordana Siljanovska-Davkova says Skopje wants guarantees that constitutional changes will not be followed by new demandsImage: Macedonian Information Agency

blocks.text: A nationally representative survey by the Institute for Democracy "Societas Civilis" illustrates the contradiction: 71% of respondents support EU membership, but only 24% back the constitutional amendments needed to advance the process. Among ethnic Macedonians, support for the amendments falls to just 11%.

Skopje-based political analyst Petar Arsovski describes the public mood as "passive-aggressive:" Strong support for joining the EU coexists with weak support for making the concession currently required to move forward.
That, he says, helps preserve the status quo.
High domestic political stakes
The dispute is now deeply embedded in domestic politics in both North Macedonia and Bulgaria, where retreat from established positions could easily be portrayed as a national defeat.
The political cost is particularly high in Skopje, where the current government came to power in part on a platform of opposition to constitutional changes under the existing conditions.
For North Macedonia's government, accepting the amendments without further guarantees carries considerable domestic political risks.
The EU, meanwhile, is not offering to reopen the negotiating framework.

The uncertainty is compounded by debate over how future EU enlargement should work. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and French President Emmanuel Macron have proposed allowing candidates to gradually gain some benefits of membership before formally joining, while stressing that full membership remains the ultimate goal.
According to Arsovski, uncertainty over the future course of enlargement gives ammunition to Eurosceptic narratives and reduces the political incentive for a difficult compromise.

"If these overall conditions remain unchanged, the most likely scenario is that EU summits come and go, while political actors remain dug in, with no real convergence of positions and no genuine commitment to a substantive compromise," Arsovski told DW.
